title: Three Questions
author: Leo Tolstoy
summary: A king feels that he would never fail if he knew three things: the right time to begin everything, the right people to listen to (and whom to avoid), and the most important thing to do. He offers a great reward to anyone who can answer.

Learned men give different answers. For the first question: draw up a timetable and keep to it; watch everything and not waste time on idle pleasures; consult a council of wise men; ask magicians. For the second: councillors, priests, doctors or warriors. For the third: science, skill in warfare, or religious worship. The king is not satisfied.

He decides to consult a hermit famous for his wisdom, who sees only simple folk. The king dresses as an ordinary man, leaves his bodyguard behind and walks to the hut. The hermit, frail and breathing heavily, is digging beds and does not answer. The king takes the spade and digs for hours.

At sunset a bearded man runs out of the wood, bleeding from a stomach wound, and faints. The king washes and bandages the wound and gives him water; tired out, he sleeps on the threshold. In the morning the man confesses that he is the king's enemy: the king had executed his brother and seized his property, and he had come to kill the king on his way back. The king's bodyguard had wounded him. Now he begs forgiveness and promises to serve the king faithfully. The king forgives him, promises to restore his property and to send his doctor.

The hermit then says the king has had his answers. Had he not stayed to dig, the man would have attacked him: so the most important time was when he was digging, the hermit was the most important man, and doing him good was the most important business. Later the wounded man was the most important person. Remember, he says, there is only one important time — Now, the only time we have power. The most important person is the one you are with, and the most important affair is to do him good.

Leo (Lev Nikolayevich) Tolstoy wrote it in Russian; it was published in What Men Live By, and Other Tales (1903), translated by the Maudes. It is a parable — a short story with human characters that teaches a moral.
Themes: living in the present, kindness and service, forgiveness turning an enemy into a friend.

Forming questions: yes/no questions (auxiliary + subject + verb), wh-questions (wh-word + auxiliary + subject + verb), questions with modals (Can/May/Should …), negative questions (Didn't you …?). Antonyms (persuade/dissuade, success/failure).

sa2: What were the three questions the king wanted answered?
What is the right time to begin everything? Who are the right people to listen to, and whom should one avoid? What is the most important thing to do?
Why was the king dissatisfied with the answers given by his ministers and learned men?
Their answers were different and contradictory — timetables, councils, magicians, priests, doctors, warriors, science, warfare or worship. None of them convinced him, so he went to the hermit.
Why did the king help the hermit dig the beds?
The hermit was old and frail and breathed heavily as he dug. Out of kindness the king offered to take the spade and dug for hours, hoping also to get his answers.
How did the king save the bearded man's life?
He washed and bandaged the man's bleeding stomach wound with his handkerchief and towel, changed the bandage till the bleeding stopped, gave him water and carried him into the hut.
Why did the bearded man ask the king's forgiveness?
He had come to kill the king, but the king had saved his life instead. Grateful and ashamed, he begged forgiveness and promised that he and his sons would serve the king faithfully.
How did the hermit prove that the king had already received his answers?

Had the king not pitied him and stayed to dig, he would have been attacked on his way back. So the digging time, the hermit and helping him were most important; later, the wounded man and caring for him were.
What is the central message of 'Three Questions'?
We should live in the present, for now is the only time we have power. The most important person is the one we are with, and the most important work is to do that person good.
sa3: Describe the change of heart in the bearded man.

He hated the king for executing his brother and seizing his property, and lay in wait to kill him. When the king tended his wound and saved his life, his hatred turned to gratitude. He begged forgiveness and vowed to serve the king; kindness turned an enemy into a friend.
What did the king learn from his visit to the hermit?

He learnt that the present is the only time that matters, that the person before us is the most important, and that doing good to that person is the most important task. He also learnt the power of kindness and forgiveness.

or: Write a character sketch of the hermit.

The hermit is wise, simple and humble. He lives in the forest and meets only ordinary people. He teaches by example rather than words, letting the king discover the answers through his own actions of kindness, and he tends the wounded stranger along with him.

sa3: It is a short, simple story with human characters that teaches a moral lesson. Through the king's experience it shows that the present moment, the person with us and doing good matter most — a lesson meant for all readers.
